[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance provides a concise, ordered starting point for Product Engineering teams tasked with implementing the Customer-Funded Customization extensibility framework. The broader documentation set — strategy white paper, 18 extension patterns, governance patterns, and the extension cookbook — is intentionally comprehensive. This document distills that material into a practical **"where to start and in what order"** reference, answering the question: *"I own a product. What do I build first to make it extensible?"*
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- Reduces ramp-up time for Product Engineering teams from weeks to days by providing a sequenced onboarding path
- Prevents common mis-sequencing mistakes (e.g., building the SDK before extension points are defined) that result in rework
- Establishes the minimum viable extension framework needed before DDI teams can begin delivering customer customizations
- Creates a shared vocabulary and mental model across product engineers, DDI teams, and Enterprise Architecture
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

- **Primary Audience**: Product Engineers and Architects responsible for making a product extensible
- **Secondary Audience**: Engineering Leads and Principal Engineers planning extensibility roadmaps
- **Stakeholders**: Product Management, DDI Leadership, Enterprise Architecture — for understanding what Product Engineering delivers at each phase

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#applicable-scenarios]

#### Applicable Scenarios

- **New Product Extensibility**: A product has no existing extension framework and needs to be built from scratch
- **Legacy Product Retrofit**: An existing product has ad-hoc or direct-code customizations that need to be migrated to the extension framework
- **Pilot Implementation**: A product has been selected as the pilot for the Customer-Funded Customization Strategy
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#scope-boundaries]

#### Scope Boundaries

- **In Scope**: What Product Engineering builds within the product to enable extensibility — extension points, plugin system, SDK, and testing harnesses
- **Out of Scope**: DDI team implementation of specific customer extensions (see [GUID-APP-IMPL-002 Extension Pattern Cookbook](./GUID-APP-IMPL-002-extension-pattern-cookbook.md)), governance processes for evaluating requests (see [GUID-GOV-PROC-000](../../governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-000-customer-change-request-process-guidance.md)), and IP ownership management (see [PTN-GOV-CUS-002](../../../../patterns/governance/customization/PTN-GOV-CUS-002-ip-ownership-classification-pattern.md))
- **Related Guidance**: [Customer-Funded Product Customization Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/customer-funded-customization-strategy.md), [GUID-GOV-PROC-001 Extension Pattern Selection](../../governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-001-extension-pattern-selection-guidance.md), [GUID-APP-IMPL-002 Extension Pattern Cookbook](./GUID-APP-IMPL-002-extension-pattern-cookbook.md)

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

- **Customer-Funded Customization Revenue**: State Medicaid agency implementations require product customizations that generate significant DDI revenue but must be managed sustainably
- **Technical Debt Crisis**: Product Engineering spends a significant portion of capacity maintaining state-specific customizations embedded in core product code, reducing innovation capacity
- **Multi-Tenant Adoption Barrier**: Current ad-hoc customization approaches are incompatible with multi-tenant architecture, blocking SaaS transformation
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#strategic-alignment]

#### Strategic Alignment

This guidance directly supports the [Customer-Funded Product Customization Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/customer-funded-customization-strategy.md), which establishes four strategic principles that Product Engineering is responsible for embodying in the product architecture:

1. **Separation of Concerns** — core product code must be independent of customer-specific logic
2. **Configuration Over Customization** — expose configuration APIs before extension points
3. **Open Extension Points** — versioned, well-defined integration contracts for customer logic
4. **Governance-First** — extension framework must support audit, approval, and lifecycle management
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#current-state-assessment]

#### Current State Assessment

- Most existing products have customer-specific logic embedded directly in core product code, often as conditional branches on state/customer identifiers
- No consistent extension interface contracts exist, meaning each customization couples tightly to product internals
- Product upgrades break customer code because there are no versioned stability guarantees
- No SDK means DDI teams re-implement boilerplate (logging, DI, configuration access) for every engagement
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#future-state-vision]

#### Future State Vision

- Products expose a catalog of **named, versioned extension points** at well-defined lifecycle hooks (pre-processing, validation, post-processing, UI injection)
- A **published SDK** (NuGet packages + `dotnet new` templates) enables DDI teams to scaffold, implement, and test extensions rapidly without deep product knowledge
- Extensions are **independently packageable and deployable** without product recompilation
- **Compatibility and isolation test suites** ship with every product release, giving DDI teams confidence their extensions still work after a product upgrade
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#problem-description]

#### Problem Description

There is no consolidated, sequenced guide for a Product Engineering team starting implementation of the extensibility framework. The existing documentation — while thorough — assumes the reader will navigate 18+ patterns, a strategy white paper, multiple governance patterns, and an implementation cookbook. Without a bootstrapping guide, teams risk:

- Starting in the wrong place (e.g., building the SDK before defining what extension points it needs to wrap)
- Building SDK components before any extension points exist in the product
- Skipping the compatibility test harness until after customer extensions are live in production
- Delivering an extension framework that DDI teams cannot actually use because there is no documentation or tooling
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#impact-assessment]

#### Impact Assessment

- Without sequencing guidance, engineering teams risk significant rework from mis-ordering (e.g., refactoring an SDK whose base classes don't match extension point contracts finalized later)
- DDI teams cannot begin customization work until Product Engineering delivers phase 1 outputs — timeline slippage cascades directly to customer delivery

| DDI Onboarding Speed | Time from SDK availability to first working extension | Track per DDI engagement | Defined per product pilot |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#principle-1-define-before-build]

#### Principle 1: Define Before Build

**Description:** Extension point interfaces and contracts must be designed and documented before any SDK, tooling, or DDI guidance is created. Everything downstream — the SDK base classes, the cookbook recipes, the DDI workflows — depends on extension point contracts being stable and well-defined.

**Rationale:** If the SDK is built before extension point contracts are finalized, the SDK must be refactored when contracts change, producing churn for both Product Engineering and early DDI adopters.

**Application:** In Phase 1, the first deliverable is always an **Extension Point Catalog** for the product — a documented list of named extension points, their interface contracts (input context, output types), execution model (sync/async, ordering), and stability guarantee. No SDK work begins until this catalog is reviewed and approved.
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#principle-2-ship-the-minimum-viable-extension-framework-first]

#### Principle 2: Ship the Minimum Viable Extension Framework First

**Description:** Resist the impulse to build the complete framework (rules engine, workflow customization, lifecycle management, frontend extensions) before validating the foundation. The minimum viable extension framework is: one or two working extension points, a usable SDK, and a compatibility test harness.

**Rationale:** The framework only delivers value when a DDI team can actually build and deploy a customer extension. Shipping a complete but untested framework late is less valuable than shipping a lean but validated foundation early.

**Application:** Phase 1 targets exactly two high-priority backend extension points (pre-processing and validation), the SDK core package, and a basic compatibility test. Everything else is Phase 2 or Phase 3.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#principle-3-test-harnesses-are-first-class-deliverables]

#### Principle 3: Test Harnesses Are First-Class Deliverables

**Description:** Compatibility testing (PTN-APP-EXT-008) and isolation testing (PTN-APP-EXT-009) harnesses must be built by Product Engineering as part of the product, not left to DDI teams. These are the mechanisms that prove extensions are safe.

**Rationale:** Without a compatibility test harness shipped by Product Engineering, each DDI team must independently validate their extensions against product upgrades — an unscalable, error-prone approach.

**Application:** Compatibility test harness ships alongside or immediately after the first extension points. It becomes part of the product's CI/CD pipeline and is updated with every product release.
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#principle-4-documentation-and-tooling-are-part-of-the-deliverable]

#### Principle 4: Documentation and Tooling Are Part of the Deliverable

**Description:** An extension framework that lacks an SDK `dotnet new` template, a "Getting Started in 30 minutes" guide, and at least one working sample extension is not complete. DDI teams cannot use an undocumented extension framework.

**Rationale:** Rapid DDI team onboarding is only achievable with templates, samples, and documentation — not just published interfaces.

**Application:** Phase 1 deliverables explicitly include an SDK quickstart guide, one sample extension per supported extension point, and a video walkthrough.
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#approach-1-bottom-up--start-with-extension-point-design]

#### Approach 1: Bottom-Up — Start with Extension Point Design

**Overview:** Begin with the product's core business workflows and identify the natural seams where customer-specific logic needs to plug in. Design extension point contracts at those seams first, then build the extension framework around them.

**When to Use:** The standard approach for all product extensibility implementations. Deviations require explicit justification.

**Implementation:**
1. Map the product's primary business workflows (e.g., claims processing pipeline, eligibility determination, provider enrollment)
2. For each workflow, identify where state-specific variations currently exist in the codebase
3. Define extension point names, input context types, output types, and execution model at each seam
4. Review contracts with at least one DDI team to validate they cover real customization needs
5. Publish contracts as interfaces in the SDK

**Benefits:** Ensures extension points are grounded in real customization needs rather than hypothetical architecture

**Considerations:** Requires collaboration with DDI teams early; may need Customization Review Board input on which extension points to prioritize
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#approach-2-leverage-existing-framework-patterns-directly]

#### Approach 2: Leverage Existing Framework Patterns Directly

**Overview:** The 18 extension patterns in `patterns/application/extensions/` provide concrete, implementation-ready guidance — including C# code samples, DI registration examples, and test harness designs. Use them directly rather than designing from scratch.

**When to Use:** All cases. Product Engineering should treat the extension patterns as specifications, not suggestions.

**Implementation:**
- [PTN-APP-EXT-001](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-001-plugin-architecture-pattern.md) defines the plugin loading and registration system
- [PTN-APP-EXT-002](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-002-extension-point-pattern.md) defines how to declare and invoke extension points
- [PTN-APP-EXT-005](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-005-dotnet-extension-sdk-pattern.md) specifies the SDK structure, NuGet packages, and `dotnet new` templates
- [PTN-APP-EXT-008](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-008-compatibility-testing-pattern.md) and [PTN-APP-EXT-009](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-009-isolation-testing-pattern.md) define test harness design

**Benefits:** Avoids reinventing solutions already solved in the pattern catalog; produces consistent, reviewable implementations

**Considerations:** Patterns are marked `draft` — engage Enterprise Architecture if gaps are found
page_texts.31:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#best-practice-1-publish-extension-point-contracts-as-a-separate-nuget-package]

#### Best Practice 1: Publish Extension Point Contracts as a Separate NuGet Package

**Description:** The extension point interfaces (`IPreClaimsProcessingExtension`, `IValidationExtension`, etc.) should be published as a dedicated, minimal NuGet package (`Gainwell.{Product}.ExtensionContracts`) separate from the full SDK.

**Rationale:** DDI teams only need the interface contracts to implement extensions — they do not need the full SDK internals. Publishing contracts separately enables the contracts to version independently and be consumed without heavyweight dependencies.

**Implementation:** Create `Gainwell.{Product}.ExtensionContracts` as a thin package containing only interfaces, context types, and result types. The full SDK (`Gainwell.Extensions.SDK.Core`) depends on this package.

**Success Indicators:** DDI teams can reference only the contracts package to implement extensions without pulling in unnecessary dependencies.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#best-practice-2-version-extension-points-from-day-one]

#### Best Practice 2: Version Extension Points from Day One

**Description:** Tag every extension point interface with an explicit version (e.g., `InterfaceVersion = new Version(1, 0)`) and document the supported version range in the product's release notes.

**Rationale:** Compatibility guarantees are meaningless without version metadata. The compatibility test harness (PTN-APP-EXT-008) relies on version metadata to determine which extension/product version combinations to test.

**Implementation:** Follow the versioning approach in [PTN-APP-EXT-017](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-017-extension-design-system-integration-pattern.md) and document in the Extension Point Catalog.

**Success Indicators:** Every extension point has a version property; the compatibility test matrix is derived automatically from version metadata.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#best-practice-3-validate-with-a-real-ddi-team-before-calling-phase-1-complete]

#### Best Practice 3: Validate with a Real DDI Team Before Calling Phase 1 Complete

**Description:** Before declaring Phase 1 done, a real DDI team should successfully build a working extension using the SDK and extension points, following only the published documentation (no hand-holding from Product Engineering).

**Rationale:** The test of whether the extension framework foundation is complete is whether an external team can independently use it. Internal developer testing is not an adequate proxy.

**Implementation:** Schedule a "DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint" at the end of Phase 1. A DDI engineer pairs with no Product Engineering support and attempts to build and deploy a simple validation extension.

**Success Indicators:** DDI engineer completes first working extension using SDK + documentation alone, without assistance from Product Engineering.
page_texts.35:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#pitfall-1-building-the-sdk-before-extension-points-are-defined]

#### Pitfall 1: Building the SDK Before Extension Points Are Defined

**Description:** Teams sometimes begin writing SDK base classes before the extension point contracts are designed. This results in SDK classes that don't match actual extension point signatures, requiring refactoring.

**Impact:** Significant rework required; SDK API churn confuses early DDI adopters and erodes trust in the framework

**Prevention:** Enforce the rule that no SDK code is written until the Extension Point Catalog is finalized and reviewed. The Extension Point Catalog is a formal Gate 1 deliverable.

**Mitigation:** If this has already occurred, freeze the SDK, finalize the extension point contracts, then align the SDK to the contracts before external release.
page_texts.36:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#pitfall-2-skipping-isolation-testing-harness]

#### Pitfall 2: Skipping Isolation Testing Harness

**Description:** Teams deprioritize isolation testing (PTN-APP-EXT-009) relative to compatibility testing, or defer it entirely to DDI teams.

**Impact:** Without isolation testing, one customer's extension can inadvertently affect another tenant's data or behavior in multi-tenant deployments — a critical production risk.

**Prevention:** Treat the isolation testing harness as a Phase 1 requirement, not a Phase 2 enhancement. Gate DDI access on isolation test harness availability.

**Mitigation:** If extensions are already live without isolation testing, prioritize building the harness as an emergency Phase 1.5 effort.
page_texts.37:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#pitfall-3-undocumented-extension-points]

#### Pitfall 3: Undocumented Extension Points

**Description:** Extension points are implemented in code but not published in an accessible Extension Point Catalog that DDI teams can discover and reference.

**Impact:** DDI teams cannot find or use extension points without asking Product Engineering for help — the framework does not scale.

**Prevention:** The Extension Point Catalog must be published and linked from the product's developer documentation before any DDI onboarding begins.

**Mitigation:** If extension points exist but are undocumented, generate the catalog from code (XML doc comments + reflection) as a fast-path and publish immediately.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#methodology-overview]

#### Methodology Overview

Product Engineering implementation of the extensibility framework follows a three-phase approach aligned with the phases defined in the [Customer-Funded Product Customization Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/customer-funded-customization-strategy.md) and the [extensions patterns README](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/README.md). Each phase has explicit gate criteria — Product Engineering must complete phase deliverables before DDI teams can begin using the extension framework from that phase.
page_texts.41:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#implementation-lifecycle]

#### Implementation Lifecycle

| Phase | Objectives | Key Activities | Deliverables |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1: Foundation | Minimum viable extension framework that DDI teams can use | Extension point design, plugin system, SDK core, compatibility + isolation testing, documentation | Extension Point Catalog, SDK NuGet packages, `dotnet new` templates, quickstart guide, sample extensions |
| Phase 2: Scale | Full framework coverage, multi-tenant support, operationalized package management | Package management, additional extension points (rules engine, workflow, UI), multi-tenant loading, expanded SDK | Full extension point coverage, multi-tenant test harness, package registry, expanded SDK helpers |
| Phase 3: Maturity | Lifecycle management, advanced capabilities, optimization | Lifecycle management, contribution-back tooling, SDK tooling refinement, advanced patterns | Lifecycle management system, contribution workflow tooling, SDK v2 |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#organizational-prerequisites]

#### Organizational Prerequisites

- **Customization Review Board established**: Governance body must exist before Product Engineering publishes extension points, as the board governs which customizations can use them
- **DDI partner team identified**: At least one DDI team must be available for Phase 1 validation (DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint)
- **Engineering capacity allocated**: Phase 1 requires a dedicated engineering focus with protected capacity; cannot be done alongside full-capacity feature development
page_texts.44:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#technical-prerequisites]

#### Technical Prerequisites

- .NET 8 SDK or higher deployed to all development environments (per enterprise .NET LTS minimum)
- Internal NuGet feed configured for publishing SDK packages (`Gainwell.*` packages) with publishing restricted to approved CI/CD service principal identities and NuGet package signing policy enforced
- CI/CD pipeline capable of running compatibility test matrices across product versions N, N-1, N-2
- Access to product source to identify existing customization seams
page_texts.45:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#process-prerequisites]

#### Process Prerequisites

- Existing ad-hoc customizations inventoried and categorized (prerequisite for knowing which extension points to prioritize)
- Extension Point design review process defined (who approves new extension point contracts before publication)
- DDI documentation portal available for publishing SDK quickstart and Extension Point Catalog
page_texts.47:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#phase-1-foundation]

#### Phase 1: Foundation

**Objectives:** Deliver a working, usable-by-DDI extension foundation for high-priority backend scenarios

**Prerequisites:** Organizational prerequisites above; customization inventory complete; Customization Review Board active

**Key Activities:**

1. **Extension Point Discovery and Design** *(complete before any implementation begins)*
   - Map product business workflows and identify customization seams using existing ad-hoc customization inventory
   - Design a minimum of 2–4 extension points covering the most common DDI customization scenarios (typically: pre-processing/data enrichment, validation, post-processing/notifications)
   - Define interface contracts: input context types, output/result types, execution model (sync/async), error handling contract
   - Publish Extension Point Catalog draft for review with DDI partner team and Enterprise Architecture
   - Reference: [PTN-APP-EXT-002](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-002-extension-point-pattern.md)

2. **Extension Framework Security Architecture** *(complete before plugin system implementation begins)*
   - Conduct threat model for the plugin loading subsystem (assembly scanning → DI registration → extension invocation) per NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PL-8
   - Perform FIPS 199 categorization of the extension framework components (the framework loads third-party code into systems processing Medicaid PHI — this is a FIPS 199 High-impact subsystem under CMS ARC-AMPE)
   - Select and document applicable NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 controls based on categorization (minimally: SI-7 Software Integrity, CM-14 Signed Components, AC-6 Least Privilege, AU-12 Audit Record Generation)
   - Engage the ISSO to validate the security architecture before implementation proceeds
   - Output: Extension Framework Security Architecture document (threat model, categorization, selected controls, ISSO sign-off)

3. **Plugin System Implementation** *(depends on: Extension Point Catalog approved; Extension Framework Security Architecture complete)*
   - Implement `ExtensionRegistry` and `IExtensionPoint<TContext, TResult>` base components
   - Implement plugin loading (assembly scanning, DI registration, priority ordering)
   - Implement load-time assembly signature verification: the plugin loader must verify the signing certificate chain and refuse unsigned or untrusted assemblies (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SI-7; NIST SP 800-218 SSDF RV.1.1)
   - Wire extension point invocations into product pipelines at identified seams
   - Reference: [PTN-APP-EXT-001](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-001-plugin-architecture-pattern.md)

4. **Extension Contracts Package** *(depends on: extension point interfaces finalized)*
   - Publish `Gainwell.{Product}.ExtensionContracts` NuGet package containing all extension point interfaces and context types
   - All extension and SDK NuGet packages must be signed using a Gainwell-controlled certificate before publication to the internal feed (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-14); extension assemblies must be strong-named
   - Establish semantic versioning policy for the contracts package

5. **SDK Core Package** *(depends on: Extension Contracts Package published)*
   - Implement `ExtensionBase`, `ValidationExtensionBase`, and other base classes
   - Implement SDK helpers: logging wrappers, configuration access, DI helpers
   - Implement `ExtensionTestBase<T>` for unit testing extensions
   - SDK packages must include a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in CycloneDX or SPDX format per NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SR-3 and federal SBOM requirements
   - Publish `Gainwell.Extensions.SDK.Core` and `Gainwell.Extensions.SDK.Testing` NuGet packages
   - Reference: [PTN-APP-EXT-005](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-005-dotnet-extension-sdk-pattern.md)

6. **`dotnet new` Templates** *(depends on: SDK Core Package stable)*
   - Create and publish `Gainwell.Extensions.Templates` package
   - Templates: validation extension, pre-processing extension, post-processing extension
   - Usage: `dotnet new gainwell-validation-ext -n "StateA.{Product}.ClaimsValidation"`
   - Reference: [PTN-APP-EXT-005](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-005-dotnet-extension-sdk-pattern.md)

7. **Compatibility and Isolation Testing Harnesses** *(can begin in parallel with SDK once extension points are wired)*
   - Build compatibility test harness that runs extension tests against product versions N, N-1, N-2
   - Build isolation test harness validating extensions do not affect core product behavior or other tenant data — this harness is a **HIPAA compliance control** (§164.312(a)(1) Access Control; NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement), not merely an engineering best practice; cross-tenant data access by an extension constitutes a reportable HIPAA breach
   - Integrate both harnesses into product CI/CD pipeline
   - Reference: [PTN-APP-EXT-008](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-008-compatibility-testing-pattern.md), [PTN-APP-EXT-009](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-009-isolation-testing-pattern.md)

8. **Security Testing** *(depends on: plugin system and SDK complete)*
   - Perform SAST scan of the plugin loading subsystem and SDK
   - Run dependency vulnerability scan of all SDK and extension contract packages (Snyk, SonarQube, or equivalent); no critical or high vulnerabilities may remain unmitigated
   - Validate threat model mitigations from Activity 2 are implemented as designed
   - Security testing results are a **Phase 1 gate requirement** — Phase 1 cannot be declared complete without passing security validation

9. **Documentation and Sample Extensions** *(depends on: SDK and templates complete)*
   - Publish Extension Point Catalog (final) to developer documentation portal
   - Write SDK quickstart guide: "Your First Extension in 30 Minutes"
   - Create at least one fully-documented sample extension per supported extension point
   - SDK quickstart must explicitly prohibit secrets in code, configuration files, or NuGet packages and demonstrate Azure Key Vault integration as the baseline secrets management pattern (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-5, SC-12)
   - Reference: [PTN-APP-EXT-005](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-005-dotnet-extension-sdk-pattern.md) SDK documentation section

10. **DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint** *(final gate before Phase 1 declared complete)*
    - DDI engineer builds and deploys first working extension using SDK + documentation only (no hand-holding)
    - DDI engineer must have completed HIPAA training before participating in the validation sprint (HIPAA §164.308(a)(5))
    - Capture friction points; resolve blockers before publishing Phase 1 complete

**Deliverables:**

- Extension Point Catalog (published)
- Extension Framework Security Architecture document (threat model, FIPS 199 categorization, NIST 800-53 control selection, ISSO sign-off)
- `Gainwell.{Product}.ExtensionContracts` NuGet package (signed, strong-named)
- `Gainwell.Extensions.SDK.Core` NuGet package (signed, with SBOM)
- `Gainwell.Extensions.SDK.Testing` NuGet package (signed, with SBOM)
- `Gainwell.Extensions.Templates` `dotnet new` template package
- Compatibility test harness (in CI/CD)
- Isolation test harness (in CI/CD) — classified as a HIPAA compliance control
- Security testing results (SAST + dependency vulnerability scan)
- SDK Quickstart Guide (including secrets management guidance and Key Vault integration)
- Sample extensions (one per extension point)

**Gate Criteria for Phase 2:** DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint succeeds; DDI engineer completes first extension without Product Engineering assistance using only published documentation. Security testing passes with no unmitigated critical or high findings. ISSO has signed off on the Extension Framework Security Architecture. **Phase 1 extensions are validated for single-tenant deployment only.** Multi-tenant production deployment requires Phase 2 completion of [PTN-APP-MTN-010](../../../../patterns/application/multi-tenancy/PTN-APP-MTN-010-tenant-extension-loading-pattern.md) (Tenant-Scoped Extension Loading).

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#critical-success-factor-1-executive-sponsorship-and-capacity-protection]

#### Critical Success Factor 1: Executive Sponsorship and Capacity Protection

**Description:** Phase 1 requires a dedicated engineering team with protected capacity (no competing sprint priorities).

**Importance:** The extension framework is not a product feature; it has no direct customer-visible output. Without capacity protection, it will be continuously deprioritized in favor of feature work.

**Implementation:** Establish a dedicated extensibility workstream with explicit roadmap allocation verified by VP Product Engineering.

**Measurement:** Track sprint velocity allocated to extensibility framework work; establish and hold a target allocation agreed with Product Engineering leadership at program outset.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#critical-success-factor-2-ddi-team-involvement-from-week-1]

#### Critical Success Factor 2: DDI Team Involvement from Week 1

**Description:** DDI teams must participate in extension point design review, not just consume the output.

**Importance:** Extension points designed without DDI input frequently miss the actual customization needs, requiring costly redesign after publication.

**Implementation:** Schedule bi-weekly check-ins with a DDI partner team throughout Phase 1; include DDI engineer in Extension Point Catalog review.

**Measurement:** DDI engineer sign-off on Extension Point Catalog before plugin system implementation begins.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#execution-steps]

#### Execution Steps

1. **Design the Extension Point Catalog** (Gate 1)
   - Use the customization inventory to identify the 2–4 highest-priority extension seams
   - For each: name it, define the C# interface signature, define input context and output types, document execution model
   - Template: See the Extension Point interface examples in [PTN-APP-EXT-002](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-002-extension-point-pattern.md) Implementation Guidelines Phase 1
   - Gate: Reviewed by Enterprise Architecture and signed off by one DDI team

2. **Implement Plugin System** (Gate 2)
   - Implement `IExtensionPoint<TContext, TResult>`, `ExtensionRegistry`, and plugin loading per [PTN-APP-EXT-001](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-001-plugin-architecture-pattern.md)
   - Wire extension point invocations into product pipeline at each seam identified in the catalog
   - Gate: At least one end-to-end test passing a simple no-op extension through the full pipeline

3. **Publish Extension Contracts Package**
   - Package all extension point interfaces and context types into `Gainwell.{Product}.ExtensionContracts`
   - Push to internal NuGet feed; document package ID and version

4. **Build and Publish SDK**
   - Implement SDK per [PTN-APP-EXT-005](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-005-dotnet-extension-sdk-pattern.md): `ExtensionBase`, validation base, logging helpers, DI helpers, test base
   - Create and publish `dotnet new` templates
   - Publish to internal NuGet feed

5. **Build Testing Harnesses**
   - Implement compatibility test harness (product version matrix: N, N-1, N-2) per [PTN-APP-EXT-008](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-008-compatibility-testing-pattern.md)
   - Implement isolation test harness per [PTN-APP-EXT-009](../../../../patterns/application/extensions/PTN-APP-EXT-009-isolation-testing-pattern.md)
   - Integrate both into CI/CD

#### Validation Steps

1. **Internal Developer Test**
   - A Product Engineering developer (not the extension framework author) follows the quickstart guide and builds a sample extension from scratch
   - Target: first working extension within a single work session using only the quickstart guide

2. **DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint**
   - An external DDI engineer follows documentation only and builds + deploys a working extension targeting a realistic customization scenario
   - Target: completed within a single sprint day; no Product Engineering assistance

3. **Compatibility Test Baseline**
   - Run the compatibility test harness against the sample extensions across the supported product version matrix
   - All tests pass before Phase 1 is declared complete

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#decision-point-1-which-extension-points-to-prioritize-in-phase-1]

#### Decision Point 1: Which Extension Points to Prioritize in Phase 1

**Context:** When more than 4 customization seams are identified in the inventory, Product Engineering must prioritize which to implement first.

**Options:** (A) Implement all seams simultaneously; (B) Prioritize by DDI request frequency; (C) Prioritize by risk of technical debt if not converted

**Criteria:** Frequency of existing customer customization at this seam; DDI team stated urgency; risk of continued ad-hoc customization; implementation complexity

**Recommendation:** Use a scoring matrix weighting DDI request frequency, technical debt risk, and implementation complexity. Implement the highest-scoring 2–4 seams in Phase 1; remainder in Phase 2. Weights should be agreed with the Customization Review Board at program outset.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#decision-point-2-frontend-extension-points--phase-1-or-phase-2]

#### Decision Point 2: Frontend Extension Points — Phase 1 or Phase 2

**Context:** For products with a React frontend, the team must decide whether to include frontend extension points in Phase 1 or defer to Phase 2.

**Options:** (A) Include frontend in Phase 1; (B) Defer frontend to Phase 2; (C) Deliver backend Phase 1 in parallel with frontend design-only (no implementation)

**Criteria:** Whether existing DDI customizations include UI modifications; product's frontend maturity (legacy vs. modern React); team's frontend expertise

**Recommendation:** Defer frontend extension implementation to Phase 2 unless the majority of identified customizations involve UI. Frontend extension patterns (Module Federation, React Component Extension) have higher implementation complexity and depend on a modern frontend stack.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#techniques-and-methods]

#### Techniques and Methods

- **Extension Point Contract Review**: Treat extension point interface definitions as public APIs — require the same review rigor as REST API contracts before publication
- **Strangler Fig for Legacy Customizations**: When migrating existing ad-hoc customizations, use the Strangler Fig pattern — route calls through the new extension point while the legacy code is still in place, then remove legacy code once the extension is validated
- **Documentation-Driven Development for SDK**: Write the SDK quickstart guide before implementing the SDK. This forces the team to define the desired developer experience first and implement to meet it.

#### Use Case 1: Claims Processing Product — Backend Extension Points Only

**Scenario Description:** A claims processing product needs to expose extension points for state-specific pre-adjudication validation rules and post-adjudication notification logic. No UI customization required.

**Context:** Product has a .NET 8 backend, existing ad-hoc state-specific code across multiple locations, active DDI engagements needing extensions within the near term

**Guidance Application:**
- Phase 1 scoped to backend only: pre-adjudication validation extension point + post-adjudication hook
- Frontend extensions deferred to Phase 2
- DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint targets a Florida-specific claims validation rule

**Adaptations:** All 18 patterns apply, but the frontend patterns (PTN-APP-EXT-012 through PTN-APP-EXT-018) are deferred

**Success Factors:** DDI team involvement in extension point contract review; compatibility test matrix covering 3 product releases

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#use-case-2-provider-enrollment-product--legacy-retrofit]

#### Use Case 2: Provider Enrollment Product — Legacy Retrofit

**Scenario Description:** A provider enrollment product has accumulated multiple state-specific code branches over several years. The product team needs to refactor these into the extension framework while keeping the product functional for all existing customers.

**Context:** No new development capacity; refactoring must be done incrementally without breaking existing deployments

**Guidance Application:**
- Use Strangler Fig approach: implement the extension framework alongside existing ad-hoc code
- Route existing customization logic through new extension points one branch at a time
- Run compatibility tests before removing each legacy branch
- Prioritize the most recently modified ad-hoc customizations (highest maintenance burden) for Phase 1 migration

**Adaptations:** Phase 1 timeline will extend due to incremental migration complexity; Extension Point Catalog includes both new and migrated extension points

**Success Factors:** Thorough regression test coverage before any legacy branch removal; DDI team validation that migrated extension matches original behavior

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#implementation-lessons]

#### Implementation Lessons

- **Extension point contracts are harder to get right than they appear**: Plan for multiple rounds of revision after initial DDI review. Budget materially more time for contract design than initial estimates suggest.
- **SDK usability trumps SDK completeness**: A simple SDK that DDI teams can use immediately is more valuable than a complete SDK delayed for exhaustive coverage. Ship core; iterate.
- **Compatibility test harness pays for itself in the first product release**: Teams that defer compatibility testing until Phase 2 consistently discover extension breakage after a product upgrade — at the worst possible time (during a DDI go-live window).

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#best-practices-discovered]

#### Best Practices Discovered

- **Treat the Extension Point Catalog as the product's public API documentation**: Maintain it with the same rigor as an OpenAPI/Swagger spec. DDI teams depend on it.
- **Include a "Known Limitations" section in the SDK quickstart**: Being honest about Phase 1 gaps (e.g., no rule engine extension yet) prevents DDI teams from attempting unsupported scenarios.
- **Create a Slack/Teams channel for DDI extension questions from day one**: Centralizes support requests, captures FAQ, and surfaces documentation gaps quickly.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#security-and-regulatory-compliance]

#### Security and Regulatory Compliance

- **Package Integrity**: All extension and SDK NuGet packages must be signed using a Gainwell-controlled certificate; extension assemblies must be strong-named. The plugin loader must verify the signing certificate chain at load time and refuse unsigned or untrusted assemblies (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SI-7, CM-14; NIST SP 800-218 SSDF RV.1.1)
- **SBOM**: SDK packages must include a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in CycloneDX or SPDX format per federal requirements (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SR-3)
- **NuGet Feed Access Control**: Publishing to the internal NuGet feed must be restricted to approved CI/CD service principal identities only; human approval workflow required for package promotion to production-consumable status; all publish and consume events must be audit-logged (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-11, AC-2)
- **Vulnerability Scanning**: Extension packages must pass dependency vulnerability scanning (Snyk, SonarQube, or equivalent) before acceptance into the internal NuGet feed; no critical or high vulnerabilities may remain unmitigated at the time of publication (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 RA-5)
- **Isolation Testing as HIPAA Control**: The isolation test harness (PTN-APP-EXT-009) is a HIPAA compliance control (§164.312(a)(1)); it must be a hard Phase 1 gate, not merely a deliverable. Cross-tenant data access by an extension constitutes a reportable HIPAA breach
- **Multi-Tenant Deployment Constraint**: Phase 1 extensions are validated for single-tenant deployment only. Multi-tenant production deployment requires Phase 2 completion of PTN-APP-MTN-010 (Tenant-Scoped Extension Loading) per NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-4, SC-4
- **Secrets Management**: Extensions must not embed API keys, credentials, or secrets in code, configuration files, or NuGet packages. The SDK must provide Azure Key Vault integration as the baseline secrets management pattern (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-5, SC-12)
- **HIPAA Training**: DDI engineers must complete HIPAA training before participating in the DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint or implementing production extensions accessing PHI-containing contexts (HIPAA §164.308(a)(5))

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#risk-assessment]

#### Risk Assessment

| Risk Category | Risk Description | Probability | Impact | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capacity Risk | Product Engineering capacity pulled back to feature work before Phase 1 complete | High | High | Executive sponsorship; protected workstream allocation |
| Contract Instability | Extension point contracts require breaking changes after DDI teams have started using them | Medium | High | Thorough DDI review before publication; enforce semantic versioning |
| Adoption Risk | DDI teams bypass extension framework and continue ad-hoc customizations | Medium | High | Governance gate: require Review Board approval for any customization; board routes to extension framework |
| Compatibility Drift | Product upgrades break extensions in production | Low (with harness) / High (without) | Critical | Make the compatibility test harness a Phase 1 non-negotiable |

| Metric | Description | Measurement Method | Target | Frequency |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md#maturity-model]

### Maturity Model

| Maturity Level | Description | Characteristics | Next Steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level 1: Ad-Hoc | No extension framework | Customer logic embedded in core product; no contracts | Begin Phase 1: extension point design |
| Level 2: Foundation | Phase 1 complete | 2–4 backend extension points live; SDK published; DDI onboarding validated | Begin Phase 2: expand coverage |
| Level 3: Scale | Phase 2 complete | Full extension point coverage (backend + frontend); multi-tenant support; package registry | Begin Phase 3: lifecycle management |
| Level 4: Mature | Phase 3 complete | Lifecycle management; contribution-back tooling; SDK v2 | Continuous improvement; optimize based on DDI feedback |
| Level 5: Optimizing | Continuous improvement active | AI-assisted extension generation; shared extension marketplace; multi-state collaboration patterns | See Future Trends in strategy white paper |
